title: Learning Standard Model structure from LHC data with Riemannian flow matching
hook: Told nothing about particle physics except one energy rule, an AI trained on a billion real LHC collisions spontaneously rediscovered known particle masses and a constant of the weak force.
key_points: ShellFlow is a generative AI model trained on about a billion real proton-proton collisions from ATLAS Open Data.
Its only built-in physics rule: a particle's energy, momentum, and mass must satisfy the 'on-shell' condition.
From that alone, it learned to reproduce known particle-pair mass peaks (J/ψ, Υ, Z boson) at their textbook positions.
It also recovered the leptonic Weinberg angle, plus the W boson and top-quark masses, unprompted.
It even reproduced correlations between particles that were never a direct training target.
Much of the Standard Model's structure turns out to be directly learnable from raw collision data alone.
content_html: Feed an AI model a billion real particle-collision events and tell it nothing about particle physics except one basic rule — and what comes out looks a lot like the Standard Model. A new generative model trained purely on LHC data spontaneously recovers known particle masses and a fundamental constant of the electroweak force, with no theory built in beyond that one constraint.
extra_html: Midori Kato, Inar Timiryasov, Oleg Ruchayskiy, and colleagues built ShellFlow, a transformer-based generative AI model that generates each particle's momentum given only which particles were recorded in an event — respecting the "on-shell" condition that a particle's energy, momentum, and mass must be mutually consistent, plus the invariant-mass formula. That's the only physics it's told. Trained on roughly a billion real proton-proton collisions from the ATLAS Open Data 13 TeV release, the model learned to reproduce the correct internal kinematics of each particle, the known dilepton resonance peaks (J/ψ, Υ, Z boson) at their textbook positions, the leptonic Weinberg angle, the W boson and top-quark masses, and correlations between particles that were never part of what it was explicitly trained to match.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

related.title: How Many Elementary Particles Are There, Really?
related.hook: Count the Standard Model's particles and you might say 17 — but tweak the rules and the tally climbs past 900, with one rigorous answer that isn't even a whole number.
